note: Synthesised from per-sign recipes, not recorded.

bohairic.note: The pronunciation of the Coptic Orthodox liturgy as it is sung today. It is not ancient: it is the product of a nineteenth-century reform, begun by Iryan Moftah around 1858 under Patriarch Cyril IV, which re-read the Greek-derived letters with their MODERN Greek values in order to bring Coptic chant closer to the Greek church. It replaced an older reading, and it is the reason a Greek voice can pronounce most of this alphabet correctly.

0.why: The Coptic name is alfa, not alpha, and the reform makes that literal: ⲫ is [f], exactly as Greek φ is. Melina reading άλφα is therefore not an approximation of the Coptic — it is the same sound chain.
0.compromise: None of consequence. But note that the name records the reform's own result: before it, this letter's third sound was an aspirated [pʰ].

1.why: Italian gives [v] initially and a clean intervocalic [d], with two pure vowels. A Greek voice reading βίδα would soften the δ to [ð] and get the wrong consonant.
1.compromise: Genuinely contested. In the liturgy the reform reads ⲇ inside Greek loanwords as [ð] — ⲇⲟⲝⲁ is chanted 'thoxa' — so a strict application would give [ˈviða]. But church alphabet charts transmit the letter's own name as 'Vida' with a plain [d], and that is what this clip gives.

2.why: The reform imported Modern Greek's value wholesale: ⲅ is the voiced velar fricative [ɣ], which is why ⲁⲅⲓⲟⲥ is sung 'aghios' and not 'agios'.
2.compromise: Modern Greek has lost its geminates, so Melina says [ˈɣama] with a single consonant where the name is spelt with two. And this hall's own alphabet states a hard [g] for ⲅ — that is the academic Sahidic convention, and it is what the Old Bohairic clip gives instead.

3.why: Italian gives a true [d] at both ends and pure [a] vowels; Spanish would fricativise the second one to [ð] and Greek both of them.
3.compromise: As with vida: the reform's value for ⲇ inside a Greek word is [ð], but the letter's name is taught with [d]. Which is 'correct' depends on whether you treat the name as a Greek word or as a piece of Coptic vocabulary.

4.why: Modern Greek γ before a front vowel is the palatal [ʝ] — the nearest available thing to the glide between the two vowels of ⲉⲓⲉ. Spelling it 'εγε' also stops the voice reading ει as a single [i], which Greek orthography would otherwise force.
4.compromise: [ʝ] is a fricative with audible friction where Coptic has a plain glide [j]. The name is really just 'e-ye'.

5.why: σου is an ordinary Greek word and gives exactly [su]; the written accent stops it being reduced as an unstressed clitic.
5.compromise: Phonetically none — but the clip is misleading if taken for a sound value. ⲋ has none. It is never used to spell a word; it carries the number six and nothing else, and this is the pronunciation of a name attached to a numeral.

6.why: Greek ζ is a plain [z], which is the reform's value for ⲍ, and no Italian or Spanish voice can begin a word with [z] at all.

7.why: Greek has no [h] whatever, so no Greek voice can say this name. Finnish has a clean [h], pure unreduced short vowels, unaspirated stops, and obligatory stress on the first syllable — which is where ϩⲁⲧⲉ takes it.
7.compromise: Finnish a is the back [ɑ] rather than a central [a]. More importantly the name is uninformative: ϩⲁⲧⲉ contains no ⲏ, so it cannot demonstrate the reform's most consequential vowel change — that ⲏ is now read [i], which is why ⲁⲙⲏⲛ is sung 'ameen'.

8.why: The reform's value for ⲑ is [θ] as in 'thin', identical to Modern Greek θ, so a Greek voice is exactly right twice over.
8.compromise: None of consequence. This is one of the loudest results of the reform: before it, ⲑ was an aspirated [tʰ], the aspirated partner of ⲧ, not a fricative at all. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

9.why: Italian initial i before a vowel is the glide [j], and Italian supplies both a clean [v] and a true [d] without softening either.
9.compromise: The [v] is the reform's reading of the digraph ⲁⲩ, which follows Modern Greek in making it [av] — the same rule that turns ⲉⲩⲗⲟⲅⲏⲙⲉⲛⲟⲥ into 'evlogimenos'. Scholarly name-lists romanise this letter 'iauda' with a diphthong, and not every teacher applies the rule inside a letter's own name. The Old Bohairic clip gives the diphthong.

10.why: Greek κ is an unaspirated [k], and so is Coptic ⲕ — it is ⲭ that carries the aspiration. An English voice saying 'kappa' would produce [kʰ] and turn ⲕ into ⲭ, collapsing a distinction the alphabet exists to make.

11.why: Italian gives two clear [l]s and takes the [vl] cluster without inserting a vowel between them.
11.compromise: Two separate uncertainties. The [v] is the reform's value for ⲁⲩ, as in iauda, and is not applied by every teacher. And the name itself is unstable in the manuscripts, which give ⲗⲁⲩⲇⲁ — straight from Greek lambda — at least as often as ⲗⲁⲩⲗⲁ.

12.why: The Coptic name is the Greek one and Greek says it correctly.
12.compromise: None. The clip cannot show the letter's most Coptic use — ⲙ̅ under the supralinear stroke, a syllable with no vowel of its own.

13.compromise: None; and as mi, the syllabic ⲛ̅ is beyond a clip of the name.

14.why: Greek begins words with [ks] naturally, where English would insert a vowel or drop the k.

15.why: Italian 'o' is a real word — the conjunction — and is read as an open short [ɔ], which is what this hall states for ⲟ ('as in got'). Written with the grave accent the voice reads the accent aloud; bare, it is clean.
15.compromise: A bare vowel is the shortest thing a synthesiser can be asked for and comes out clipped. And under the reform ⲟ and ⲱ have merged in quality — both are [o] — so nothing in this clip distinguishes them; only the Old Bohairic pair does.

16.why: Greek π is unaspirated and so is Coptic ⲡ. English 'pea' would give [pʰ], which in Coptic is a different letter, ⲫ.

17.why: Greek gives a single clean tap and a pure [o].
17.compromise: Modern Greek r is a tap; Coptic ⲣ was more likely a fuller trill or flap, and in native words it can be syllabic under the stroke, which no clip of a name can show.

18.why: Greek initial σ is [s] and the vowels are pure. σίμα is close enough to a real Greek word that the stress is reliable.

19.why: Coptic church charts romanise this letter 'Tav': under the reform ⲁⲩ is [av]. Italian gives an unaspirated [t] — Coptic ⲧ is unaspirated, ⲑ is the aspirate — and a clean final [v].
19.compromise: A Greek voice reading ταυ gives [taf], because Modern Greek devoices the digraph before a pause or a voiceless sound. Coptic does not consistently follow it there, and cantors vary between 'tav' and 'taf'. The clip commits to [tav].

20.why: Written as two words to hold the hiatus of ⲟⲩⲁ. Run together, both Greek and Italian would collapse it into the glide [wa] and lose the first syllable entirely.
20.compromise: The pause between the words is considerably longer than the hiatus warrants — the clip runs close to two seconds for two short syllables. Note too that ⲩ almost never stands alone in native words: its real work is the digraph ⲟⲩ, which writes both [u] and [w]. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

21.why: The reform's value for ⲫ is [f], which is what Greek φ is — hence ⲫⲛⲟⲩϯ sung as 'efnouti'.
21.compromise: None of consequence. But the letter's name in this hall is 'fi', not 'phi', and that spelling is itself the record of the change: the older value was an aspirated [pʰ].

22.why: The reform's value for ⲭ in Greek words is Modern Greek χ, and before a front vowel that is the palatal fricative [ç].
22.compromise: The name happens to catch the palatal allophone; before a back vowel the same letter is the velar [x], as in ⲡⲓⲭⲣⲓⲥⲧⲟⲥ. And in native Coptic words — where ⲭ stands for ⲕ before ϩ — the reform reads it simply as [k], so this clip covers only one of the letter's two lives.

23.why: Greek begins words with [ps] without difficulty; English cannot.

24.why: Two words to keep ⲱⲟⲩ in two syllables — as one word Greek would read it as a single [ou]. The slow rate lengthens the ⲱ.
24.compromise: The pause is too long, and rate is a crude stand-in for vowel length: it slows the whole utterance, not the vowel alone. Under the reform ⲱ and ⲟ have merged in quality exactly as they have in Modern Greek, so the length heard here is historical, not something a cantor observes. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

25.why: The first of the Demotic letters, and unspellable in Greek: Greek has no [ʃ] and no voice reading Greek can produce one. Italian 'sciai' is a real Italian word (skis) pronounced [ʃai] — the sound and the diphthong together, exactly.
25.compromise: None of consequence. This is the cleanest recipe in the hall.

26.why: 'fai' is a real Italian word with a true falling diphthong [ˈfai]. A Greek spelling would be hopeless here: Greek αι is read [e], so φαι would come out 'fe'.

27.why: Castilian j is a strong voiceless back fricative and Spanish 'ai' is a clean diphthong. Coptic teaching identifies this letter's sound with Arabic خ, which is what Spanish j most nearly is among the voices available.
27.compromise: Castilian j is often uvular [χ] rather than velar [x]. For ϧ, which descends from Egyptian ẖ and is taught by analogy with Arabic خ, that backing is arguably nearer the target than a plain velar would be — but it is not the target. Note also that ϧ is a Bohairic letter only: Sahidic had already merged this sound into ϩ.

28.why: Finnish is the only voice here that combines a clean [h] with pure unreduced vowels, an apical r, and fixed first-syllable stress. Greek and Italian have no [h] at all; German would give a uvular r, English would colour the vowels.
28.compromise: Finnish r is a full trill where Coptic ⲣ is more likely a tap. Nothing else available gets the [h] without a worse cost elsewhere.

29.why: Italian gi before a is [dʒ] — the reform's value for ϫ, taught as 'j as in judge' — and Italian keeps the internal [n] before the second affricate without nasalising the vowel away.
29.compromise: This is the Bohairic reading. Sahidic ϫ is normally reconstructed as a palatal stop [c] or an unaspirated [tʃ] — the hall's 'palatal ty' — and the Old Bohairic clip gives that instead.

30.why: 'cima' is a real Italian word, [ˈtʃiːma] — the reform's value for ϭ, taught as 'ch as in church'.
30.compromise: Italian lengthens the stressed i. More substantially, this reading is late: historically ϭ is not an independent [tʃ] at all but the ASPIRATED partner of ϫ, in the same relation ⲫ ⲑ ⲭ stand to ⲡ ⲧ ⲕ. The hall's 'palatalised k' is the Sahidic value, and the Old Bohairic clip attempts the aspirate.

31.why: Italian t is unaspirated and Italian i is pure, so 'ti' is the plain [ti] this letter writes. English 'tea' would aspirate it into something Coptic would spell ⲑ.
31.compromise: None of consequence. This is the one sign in the alphabet that is a whole syllable rather than a sound, so the name and the value are the same thing — the only letter where the clip is the letter.

32.why: The same sound and the same name as ϧ, so the same recipe: Castilian j for the back fricative, Spanish 'ai' for the diphthong.
32.compromise: As ϧ, the Spanish fricative is likely uvular rather than velar. Beyond that, this clip is an anachronism by construction: ⳉ is an Akhmimic sign, and Akhmimic has no liturgical tradition and no reformed pronunciation — nobody has ever chanted this letter in a Coptic church. It is voiced here only because the sound it writes is one that Bohairic also had.

old.note: How the letters were read before the nineteenth-century reform: reconstructed from philology, and supported by the traditional pronunciation that survived into the twentieth century in Upper Egyptian villages after Greco-Bohairic had taken the churches. Its organising fact is a series of aspirates — ⲫ ⲑ ⲭ ϭ against ⲡ ⲧ ⲕ ϫ — that the reform dissolved into fricatives and affricates. Vowel length is real here: ⲏ and ⲱ are long against ⲉ and ⲟ.

0.why: The name is spelt with ⲫ, and before the reform ⲫ was an aspirated [pʰ], not [f] — so the Coptic name was the Greek name, alpha. Italian gives two pure [a] vowels and a [p]; English would give [ˈælfə], wrong in the vowel, the consonant and the ending at once.
0.compromise: No synthesiser aspirates a stop in the middle of a word, so this is a plain [p] where an aspirated [pʰ] is wanted. The clip is right about the letter and short of breath about it.

1.why: Before the reform ⲃ was a labial stop and ⲏ a long [eː], so the name was 'beda' — the Greek beta barely changed. Italian gives [b], a pure [e] and a true [d]; the slow rate lengthens the vowel.
1.compromise: Rate is a crude stand-in for phonemic length. And the reconstruction is contested: ⲃ may already have been the bilabial fricative [β] in much of Coptic, which is a sound no voice here can produce. The letter's own Coptic name — vida, not beta — is evidence that the shift toward [v] was under way long before Moftah.

2.why: A hard [g], which is the value this hall's alphabet states, with a genuine Italian geminate for the doubled ⲙ. Melina would give [ˈɣama] — the reform's fricative, and no geminate.
2.compromise: ⲅ occurs almost only in Greek loanwords, so its Coptic value tracked whatever Greek was doing at the time the word was borrowed — [g] early, [ɣ] increasingly later. 'Old Bohairic ⲅ' is therefore less a single sound than a date.

3.why: Unchanged from the other system: Italian gives a true [d] at both ends and pure vowels.
3.compromise: None of consequence here — the uncertainty about ⲇ belongs to the reformed reading, where [ð] competes with [d]. Before the reform the letter was a plain stop.

4.why: Unchanged: the reform did not touch ⲉ, and Greek γ before a front vowel remains the closest available thing to the glide in ⲉⲓⲉ.
4.compromise: As in the other system: [ʝ] is a fricative where a plain glide [j] is wanted.

5.compromise: As in the other system: the letter has no sound value in any period. It was already a bare numeral in Greek before Coptic took it.

6.why: Unchanged: ⲍ was [z] before the reform as after it, and Greek is the only voice here that can begin a word with [z].

7.why: The NAME is unchanged — Finnish [h], pure vowels, first-syllable stress — even though the letter's value is not.
7.compromise: Finnish a is the back [ɑ]. And the name still fails to demonstrate the letter: ϩⲁⲧⲉ contains no ⲏ, so the one thing worth hearing here — that before the reform ⲏ was a long [eː] and not the [i] of today's 'ameen' — is not in the clip at all.

8.why: ⲑ was the aspirated partner of ⲧ, an aspirated stop [tʰ] and not a fricative. English word-initial t is genuinely aspirated and nothing else available is; a British voice is used because an American one would flap the medial t.
8.compromise: Only the first ⲑ comes out aspirated — no synthesiser aspirates a stop after the stress, so the second is a plain [t]. The vowels are English [ɛ] rather than a long [eː]. Half of what the clip is for survives.

9.why: Italian initial i before a vowel is [j], Italian au is a true falling diphthong, and Italian d is a true [d]. Before the reform imported Greek's [av] rule, ⲁⲩ here was a diphthong.
9.compromise: None of consequence. Which of the two readings a given teacher uses for this name is not fully settled, which is why both systems carry a version.

10.why: Unchanged, and load-bearing: ⲕ is the UNaspirated member of the pair whose aspirate is ⲭ, and Greek κ is unaspirated. An English 'kappa' would say [kʰ] and produce ⲭ.

11.why: As iauda: Italian gives the diphthong [au̯] intact, and two clear [l]s.
11.compromise: The name is unstable in the manuscripts, which give ⲗⲁⲩⲇⲁ — straight from Greek lambda — at least as often as ⲗⲁⲩⲗⲁ. This clip pronounces the form the hall states.

14.why: Unchanged: Greek takes the [ks] cluster word-initially without help.

15.why: Italian 'o' is read as an open short [ɔ] — the short vowel that stood against long ⲱ before the two merged.
15.compromise: A bare vowel comes out clipped. The contrast this clip exists to make is only audible against ⲱⲟⲩ, which is deliberately slowed.

16.why: Unchanged, and structural: ⲡ is unaspirated against aspirated ⲫ, and Greek π is unaspirated. Play this against the ⲫ clip in this system to hear the pair.

17.compromise: Modern Greek gives a single tap; a fuller trill is likelier for Coptic ⲣ, and Italian would supply one at the cost of a less pure vowel.

19.why: Italian gives an unaspirated [t] — ⲧ is the plain stop against aspirated ⲑ — and a genuine falling [au̯]. Before the reform ⲩ in this position was the glide [w], not [v]; a Greek voice would say 'taf' and an English one would both aspirate and flatten the diphthong.

20.why: Unchanged: two words to hold the hiatus, which either voice would otherwise collapse to [wa].
20.compromise: The pause is far longer than the hiatus warrants. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

21.why: ⲫ was the aspirated partner of ⲡ, a true [pʰ]. English word-initial p is genuinely aspirated and nothing else here is. This is the single most important clip in the system: it is the difference between the old reading and 'efnouti'.
21.compromise: English lengthens and slightly diphthongises the vowel where the Coptic is a plain [i]. Note also that the shift of [pʰ] to [f] was not the reform's doing — Greek had made the same shift centuries earlier, and Coptic scribes' spellings show it happening in Egypt too.

22.why: ⲭ was the aspirated partner of ⲕ, a true [kʰ]. English initial k gives that; Greek χι gives the fricative [ç], which is the reformed value.
22.compromise: The English vowel is a long [iː] rather than a plain [i]. And in Greek loanwords ⲭ may already have been the fricative [x] at the same date it was still [kʰ] in native words — the letter did two jobs at once.

24.why: Two words to hold ⲱⲟⲩ in two syllables; the slow rate lengthens the ⲱ, which here is a genuinely long [oː] standing against the short ⲟ — a distinction the reform abolished.
24.compromise: The pause is too long, and rate slows the whole utterance rather than the vowel alone. It is the only handle available on phonemic length. — recipe corrected after review: the earlier one did not produce this sound.

25.why: Unchanged. The Demotic letters were never Greek, so the reform had no Greek value to give them; Italian 'sciai' is [ʃai] exactly.

26.why: Unchanged. A real Italian word with a true falling diphthong.
26.compromise: None of consequence. Worth noting that ϥ is the one letter here whose [f] is original — ⲫ only arrived at that sound later, which is why Coptic needed both.

27.why: Unchanged: a Demotic letter for a sound Greek could not write, so there was nothing for the reform to Hellenise.
27.compromise: Castilian j is often uvular [χ] rather than velar [x]. ϧ is Bohairic only — Sahidic had merged the sound into ϩ — so this letter is one of the readiest tests of dialect on a page.

28.why: Unchanged. Finnish supplies [h], pure vowels and initial stress; Greek and Italian have no [h] at all.
28.compromise: Finnish r is a trill where a tap is likelier.

29.why: 'ciancia' is a real Italian word giving [ˈtʃantʃa] — an UNASPIRATED affricate, which is the point: ϫ is the plain member of the pair whose aspirate is ϭ, exactly as ⲡ ⲧ ⲕ stand to ⲫ ⲑ ⲭ. The reform's voiced [dʒ] is later.
29.compromise: Whether the sound was an affricate [tʃ] or a plain palatal stop [c] is genuinely disputed, and this hall's alphabet states the palatal reading for Sahidic. An Italian voice can only give the affricate.

30.why: ϭ is the aspirated partner of ϫ — the fourth member of the aspirate series that gives this whole system its shape. English initial ch carries some aspiration; Italian 'cima' carries none, which is why the reformed clip uses Italian and this one does not.
30.compromise: This is the weakest recipe in the hall and should be treated as such. English ch is only weakly aspirated, and no synthesiser available can produce a properly aspirated affricate [tʃʰ] at all; the final vowel is English [ɑː] rather than a pure [a]. What you hear is an ordinary English 'cheema' gesturing at a sound the machine cannot make. The hall's alternative description — a palatalised k, [kʲ] — is the Sahidic value and is equally out of reach.

31.why: Unchanged. Italian t is unaspirated, so this is the plain [ti] the sign writes; ϯ is a syllable, not a sound, and was so in every period.

32.why: The same sound and name as ϧ, and the same recipe.
32.compromise: Castilian j is likely uvular rather than velar. And the label is a stretch: ⳉ is Akhmimic, not Bohairic, so 'Old Bohairic ⳉ' names a reading no Bohairic reader ever had to make. The honest claim is narrower — this is roughly the back fricative that Akhmimic wrote with this sign and Bohairic wrote with ϧ.
